organization_or_origin: Army Service Forces / Army Information Branch

description.summary: A poster-newspaper hybrid: one dominant map or several campaign maps surrounded by short news columns, datelines, numbered captions, monochrome photographs, inset maps, legends, week labels, and morale-building text. The look is urgent, public-information-oriented, and mechanically printed, with restrained wartime colors, dense annotation, and blunt graphic hierarchy.
description.design_principle: Make the map read like a weekly war-room newspaper broadside: strategic geography first, short dispatches second, photos and insets as evidence, all in a disciplined poster grid.
description.historical_context: The core reference is the U.S. War Department / Army Information Branch Newsmap series: weekly poster-size sheets published from 1942 to 1946 to inform and motivate service members, commonly combining maps of the previous week's military events with news briefs, photographs, graphics, and training or morale material. Related civilian/commercial news-map broadsides used a similar newspaper-poster grammar for public war news and home-front topics. government poster lithography / offset lithography newsprint halftone reproduction for photographs limited spot-color printing, often black plus muted red/orange/green/blue
geographic_origin: Army Service Forces / Army Information Branch

typography.character: Condensed newspaper sans and slab/serif headline hierarchy. Titles are blocky, compressed, and loud; body copy is small newspaper serif or utilitarian sans; map labels are all-caps or small caps with practical military clarity.
typography.fallback_strategy: Prefer metrically stable, licensable fonts with the language coverage required by the map; preserve hierarchy when substitution is necessary.
rules: Use a dominant masthead such as NEWSMAP, WAR NEWS MAP, or THE WAR THIS WEEK, but avoid exact issue imitation unless requested.
Use short active headlines: 'Allies Push Inland', 'Air Offensive Expands', 'Pacific Bases Tighten Ring'.
Body text should be arranged in narrow newspaper columns with justified or near-justified copy.
Use boxed captions, issue numbers, and source notes such as 'Prepared from public sources of information' for authenticity.
Never use playful retro display fonts; this is emergency public information, not a diner menu.

linework: Crisp black or dark gray linework with uneven print texture. Boundaries and graticules are thin; arrows, front lines, and callout boxes are assertive. Lines should look drafted and mechanically reproduced, not anti-aliased to death.
national boundaries: thin black/gray solid or dashed lines, 0.5-1 px
occupied or contested areas: flat fill plus dashed outline or hatching
front lines: bold dashed or toothed line with labels and dates
uncertain positions: dotted or stippled line with explicit uncertainty note
oceans in very pale blue/gray or paper tone
rivers thin and simplified; only include if relevant to campaign explanation
nautical routes as dashed lines with arrowheads or ship/anchor icons
railways as black lines with short ticks if central to logistics
major roads/routes as thin dark lines; omit modern highway symbology
supply routes as dashed arrows or segmented lines
air routes as arced dashed lines with aircraft silhouettes
use sparse hachures or hill shading for local campaign insets
avoid modern DEM hillshade unless posterized and converted to halftone/stipple
strategic world maps usually have little/no terrain

required: Make the map read like a weekly war-room newspaper broadside: strategic geography first, short dispatches second, photos and insets as evidence, all in a disciplined poster grid.
preferred: Build a newspaper-poster composition with a dominant map plus text/photo/inset panels.
Key map symbols to numbered news items or captions.
Include at least one inset map or photo/caption panel for full Newsmap flavor.
Do not turn the style into generic 'old parchment map' fantasy; this is mass-printed war information.
Do not present propaganda claims as factual analysis unless the map is explicitly labeled as a historical facsimile or interpretive style.
Use CSS grid for the whole broadsheet: masthead row, map field, inset/photo/news modules, footer/source line.
For MapLibre/web map library outputs, hide default zoom controls or restyle as black-on-paper square buttons.
Desktop: full broadsheet landscape layout with map occupying 50-65% of visual area.
Tablet: preserve poster frame; stack side panels beneath map if necessary.
Mobile portrait: switch to scrollable broadsheet sections with masthead, map, dispatches, insets, and legend; avoid shrinking body text below usability.
Mobile landscape: keep map dominant and put dispatch/photo panels in a bottom strip.
avoid: British Ministry of Information pictorial maps

pure RGB red/blue partisan modern palettes
large black-white-red schemes that evoke Axis propaganda rather than U.S. Newsmap style
unsupported: Exact facsimile reproduction of a named source map, protected artwork, logo, seal, interface, or trade dress.

accessibility.color_independence: Because the historical palette is low-contrast and ink-limited, pair color with hatching, labels, arrows, and numbered references. Do not rely on red/green alone for meaning.
accessibility.contrast: Preserve readable contrast for labels, lines, and critical symbols at intended zoom levels.
accessibility.minimum_text_size: Adapt historical or print typography to a practical screen-reading threshold.
additional: Test the compiled style in grayscale and under common color-vision simulations.
